analysis.one_liner: Adds fertility treatment, including IVF, to the health plans required to cover it under the ACA.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was introduced with no cosponsors and died in committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Affordable Care Act's list of 'essential health benefits' — the services that ACA-compliant health plans must cover — to add fertility treatment and care. That includes IVF, egg and sperm preservation, artificial insemination, embryo genetic testing, fertility medications, and gamete donation, and it would apply regardless of whether someone has an infertility diagnosis. Plans would have had to start covering these services about a year after enactment. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy ACA marketplace plans or coverage through small-group plans, including those facing infertility or needing fertility care, who currently often pay $10,000–$20,000 or more out of pocket per IVF cycle. Fertility clinics and makers of fertility drugs would also gain a much larger covered market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing IVF and fertility care

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'fertility treatment and care' as a required essential health benefit under the ACA, covering oocyte, sperm, and embryo preservation; artificial insemination; assisted reproductive technology including IVF; embryo genetic testing; fertility medications; and gamete donation [S2].
Coverage would apply regardless of whether the individual has a diagnosis of infertility, so people preserving fertility before cancer treatment or other medical reasons would also be covered [S2].
The requirement would take effect for plan years beginning one year after enactment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers offering ACA-compliant individual and small-group plans, and their members through premiums, since fertility treatment — especially IVF — is among the most expensive medical services. Large self-insured employer plans are generally not bound by the ACA's essential health benefit rules, so most workers with large-employer coverage would not benefit.

drawbacks.text: Mandating coverage of IVF and related services would raise premiums in ACA-compliant individual and small-group plans, spreading the high cost of fertility care across all enrollees, including those who will never use it [S2].

The ACA's essential health benefit requirement generally does not bind large self-insured employer plans, so the many Americans covered through large employers would not get the new coverage even if the bill passed — a limitation the bill does not address [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in six people who experience infertility, plus those preserving fertility before medical treatment, the benefit is large: IVF routinely costs five figures per cycle and is often excluded from coverage entirely. The cost is higher premiums spread across plan enrollees, which is how any mandated benefit works. The bill's main design weakness is its reach — it does nothing for most workers on large self-insured employer plans, the largest source of private coverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lauren Underwood introduced the bill on November 15, 2024, in the closing weeks of the 118th Congress [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S4].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S3].
The bill would have amended the ACA's essential health benefits to require coverage of fertility treatment and care, including IVF, regardless of an infertility diagnosis [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and large employers avoided a new mandate to cover expensive fertility services; no one gained the coverage the bill would have provided.

for.name: Rep. Lauren Underwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill adding fertility treatment, including IVF, to the ACA's required benefits; recruited no cosponsors before the Congress ended.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to her committee; it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors joined from either party and no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested.

industries.note: Insurers offering ACA-compliant plans would have had to cover IVF and other fertility services, among the costliest benefits in medicine, raising plan costs. A mandate of this kind generally means higher premiums across all enrollees.

industries.industry: Fertility clinics and assisted reproduction providers
industries.note: A broad coverage mandate would turn many out-of-pocket fertility patients into insured patients, greatly expanding the market for IVF and related services.
The bill requires coverage of fertility medications, including some available over the counter, expanding the covered market for these drugs.

The ACA's essential health benefit rules generally do not apply to large self-insured employer plans, so most large employers would be unaffected — meaning their workers would also go without the new coverage.
